summary: Describes a mechanism for mixing additional master secret inputs into TLS and DTLS key derivation. It is an Experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: When two people make a secret code, they can mix in extra ingredients so it is harder for anybody to guess. This lets TLS stir in extra ingredients when it builds its secret key.

questions: mixing data into tls key derivation
subtitle: Allowing TLS extensions to contribute additional data to the master secret.

tldr.problem: Some TLS extensions want to mix additional data into the calculation of the master secret, the foundation of the encrypted session, but TLS had no standard way to do this.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6358 defines a framework allowing TLS and DTLS extensions to specify additional input values that get mixed into the pseudorandom function (PRF) calculation during master secret derivation. Multiple extensions can contribute input in type-order.
tldr.outcome: This allows extensions to cryptographically bind their data directly into the session key, ensuring that any use of such an extension affects all subsequent encryption in the session.

today: RFC 6358 is Experimental. It provides a general framework that TLS extensions can use if they need additional cryptographic binding. However, adoption has been limited; most TLS extensions do not require additional master secret input.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6358 describes a lightweight extension mechanism for TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2. Some extensions need to ensure their data influences the master secret—the fundamental secret from which all session encryption keys are derived. Without this mechanism, an extension's data might be negotiated but could be ignored if the master secret calculation does not depend on it.

The solution is to allow extensions to contribute additional input to the master secret calculation. This creates a cryptographic binding: if an extension provides data, that data becomes inseparable from the session keys.
sections.eli5: TLS creates secret codes for conversations. Some extra options want to say: use my data too, so no one can ignore me. This framework lets them do that.

sections.title: The Mechanism
sections.content:
An extension that uses this framework is called an extension with master secret input. Each such extension specifies what additional data it wants mixed in. When deriving the master secret, all such extensions are sorted by type order, and their input values are concatenated with the client and server random values into the pseudorandom function.

The modified master secret formula becomes: PRF(pre_master_secret, "master secret", ClientHello.random + additional_inputs_from_client + ServerHello.random + additional_inputs_from_server)[0..47]. This ensures both client and server see the same master secret derivation.
sections.eli5: The secret recipe becomes: mix the client's random number, the extra ingredients from any options, the server's random number, and the extra ingredients from the server's options. Stir them all together.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
Adding more data to the master secret calculation gives attackers more input to potentially influence. However, TLS's pseudorandom function is designed to be indifferent to input size and to work correctly even when input contains predictable material.

Even if the additional master secret input contains no entropy or is completely predictable to an attacker, TLS still functions correctly. The pseudorandom function will generate distinct keying material for each connection regardless, so predictable additional input causes no harm to the resulting keys.
sections.eli5: Bad people might try to guess the extra ingredients, but TLS is strong enough that guessing does not help them. Even if they know what the extra ingredients are, the secret is still safe.
